strengths: Significance: PMVB provides a practical interface between solution predictors and commercial MIP solvers using two cardinality constraints. Exhaustively solving the four complementary regions preserves global optimality independently of prediction accuracy. This low integration burden is useful for repeatedly solving related instances.

Originality and soundness: Using aggregate prediction accuracy to calibrate branching neighborhoods offers an interpretable extension of local branching. Theorem 3.1's Chebyshev argument is valid under its stated population mean and variance conditions and avoids requiring independent variable errors.

Empirical merits: The experiments cover logistic regression and GNN predictors, two commercial solvers, several combinatorial problem families, and simulated unit-commitment instances. Table 2 reports potentially useful 1.11–1.31× speedups for exact solving, separately from the larger primal-heuristic gains.

Presentation, reproducibility, and limitations: Algorithm 1 explains the basic mechanism clearly, and the manuscript supplies dataset-generation settings, hardware information, and a code link. The authors appropriately acknowledge the strong independence assumption and possible data-free infeasibility. No material research-ethics concerns are apparent from the reported experiments. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-01/reviews/b08/review-experiment-ss335lnf/call-c7a639eb4d6a47cfac5a859b190548eb/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: Soundness: Theorem 2.1 is not established by its proof. Lemma 2.1 bounds prediction error averaged over instances, whereas Eq. (4) applies that bound to a fixed instance and variables selected into U or L by their predictions. High marginal accuracy does not imply high accuracy conditional on predicting 1 or 0; rare positive predictions could all be incorrect. Furthermore, A4's independence for fixed instances does not establish the independence needed after averaging over shared instance/training randomness and selecting prediction-dependent subsets. These gaps undermine the central high-probability retention guarantee.

Soundness and calibration: Theorem 3.1 requires population accuracy means and a valid variance upper bound. The manuscript does not supply finite-sample uncertainty control for estimating these quantities and selecting the threshold. Remark 3.1's stronger constraints based on raw prediction probabilities require additional calibration assumptions. Moreover, Section 5.2 uses delta = 0.8, providing only a 20% individual lower bound and no nontrivial joint guarantee for the two constraints. Empirical optimal-solution coverage is not reported, and some training labels allow a 10% optimality gap.

Evaluation and significance: Section 5.4 excludes instances where PMVB's restricted problem is infeasible and cases where both runs time out, retaining 57 of the original 132 MIPLIB instances. Excluding failures caused by the heuristic makes the reported 16% improvement a selected-subset result. A convincing benchmark evaluation should include every instance, failure counts, solution quality, and the cost of detecting failure and falling back to the original solver.

Evaluation: Section 5.2 measures time to a target selected by PMVB's own 120-second run while allowing the baseline 3600 seconds. This measures a particular time-to-target advantage, but without equal-budget objective gaps or primal-integral curves, the large speedup ratios do not establish broadly superior optimization performance. The exact-solving results lack repeated-seed results or uncertainty estimates, and the SCUC evaluation has only five test instances per setting.

Originality and attribution: The manuscript cites prediction-based distance cuts [13], local branching [14], and multivariable branching [16,54], but compares primarily against unmodified solvers. Comparisons using the same predictor with established neighborhood constraints, together with ablations of statistical threshold selection and objective cuts, are needed to isolate the contribution of probabilistic calibration.

Reproducibility and presentation: Important details remain unspecified, particularly how the variance parameter is obtained without training data, solver versions, complete benchmark membership, and whether prediction/root-LP computation is included in timings. Section 3.2 also reverses its pruning condition: if the preferred region excludes every global optimum, at least one complementary region remains feasible under the incumbent objective cut. This does not invalidate exhaustive enumeration, but the explanation of efficient pruning needs correction.
